newsitem.title: UK: Dollar/yen eases as U.S.-Japan trade tension grows.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/yen eases as U.S.-Japan trade tension grows.

text.p: The dollar was weaker against the yen in morning Europe, pressured by Japan's widening trade surplus with the U.S. and reports that Japanese life insurer Kampo was turning cautious on foreign bonds in the wake of recent Finance Ministry comments.
Japan's March overall trade surplus fell sharply but posted an 11.2 percent rise with the U.S., heightening trade tension between the two countries.
U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers warned overnight of trade friction unless Japan became less reliant on exports and promoted growth from within.

The focus now is on U.S. trade data for February due 1230 GMT with an average of analysts' forecasts pointing to an overall deficit of $10.1 billion, down from January's $12.7 billion shortfall. But attention will be on the U.S.-Japan gap with many expecting continued widening.
Dollar/yen stood at 125.30/40 yen at 0755 GMT after testing down to 125 yen earlier and down from 125.62/72 late Wednesday.

"Intervention is still a concern, and there is a lot of political will out there to make sure dollar/yen doesn't go too much higher, particularly with the attention on U.S.-Japan trade data," said Adrian Davies, senior analyst at SGST in London.
Comments from senior Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara on Wednesday that there was growing political pressure to raise Japan's official discount rate also weighed on dollar/yen.

"As time progresses and the economy looks like coming out of recession, this pressure to raise rates will increase and will go a long way to take the pressure off dollar/yen," said Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull's Davies.

Responding to earlier reports that Kampo had turned cautious on foreign bonds, a Kampo official said they were now closely watching forex moves but it did not necessarily mean they would stop investing in foreign bonds.

The mark was firmer but off highs on its European crosses. Italian press reports that Germany and France will try to reach a consensus by September over which countries participate at the start of EMU served to provide mark support.
"The story is still vague but if true, and Italy and Spain are excluded, the mark will benefit," said a UK bank dealer. "But the idea of a broad-based EMU start is still the dominant sentiment."
Sterling firmed slightly on the dollar and mark after lower-than-forecast UK inflation data.
Dollar/mark was firmer on the back of a drop in German economic institute Ifo's March index, which fell to 92.4 compared with 93.6 in February, far below expectations for a figure around 94.0.
Analsyts said the Ifo drop dispelled some of optimism in the German economy seen at the start of the year and made the prospect of higher German rates even more remote.
A nominal five percent year-on-year drop in German retail sales for February also dampened mark sentiment.
Dollar/mark was trading at 1.7269/74 after moving above 1.7280 marks earlier. It stood at 1.7281/86 late Wednesday.
